413.t: Hinton on young Black musicians not knowing their history
413.s: Hinton explains why Maxwell's oral history matters and asks why young Black musicians know little about Armstrong, Morton and Blanton.
413.ch: Young players, schools and studio work
413.q: Yeah. This is a continuation of that great session we were having talking with you. That's a beautiful story you were talking about there. And I just happened to mention to you in our conversation while we were setting up the tapes about some situations I'm sure you've been involved in and you've…

413.t: Harold Ashby and the Ben Webster solo; why young Black musicians lack time for history
413.s: Ashby does not know Webster's Congo Brava solo; Maxwell blames economics, not indifference.
413.ch: Young players, schools and studio work
413.q: Well, it came about I had written -- transcribed some arrangements for Mercer Ellington that had been lost after Duke's death. And one was on "Congo Brava" and Ben Webster made a classic tenor solo that was famous with most musicians. And I had just written in the chord symbols, I didn't write it…

413.t: Black stars not reviving older music; teachers courting popularity
413.s: Hinton asks why white players revive Morton while Black stars do not; Maxwell blames teachers seeking popularity.
413.ch: Young players, schools and studio work
413.q: I think that you can't criticize the black teachers any more than you criticize white teachers, because all teachers nowadays, black or white in any subject, seem to be more interested in conducting a popularity contest with the young people rather than trying to direct them, which a teacher should…

121.t: Young black musicians cannot play the blues
121.s: Ridgley laments that young New Orleans black musicians in 1986 don't know blues or read, so he hires white players.
121.q: Yeah, well I was talking about the present drummer that I have in my present band today, and I stated just a minute ago that I have been associated with better musicians in all of my days, and I'm talking about from way back with doing the Earl Palmer era with David Tholomew, Ernest MacLange,…

313.t: Nicholas Payton and the Doc Cheatham duet album
313.s: Young black musicians lack the foundation; Payton is the exception, and led to the Grammy-winning Stardust duets with Cheatham.
313.q: Oh yes it’s certainly true. But there’s a reason for it, which is a very unfortunate one. And that is that the younger white musicians don’t know the foundation of what they consider their music. They simply don’t go into it and—

640.t: Young Black musicians and classic jazz
640.s: Discussion of why few young Black musicians play classic jazz; she blames missing education, not color, and mentions Wynton Marsalis and Michael White.
640.ch: Race, education and the future of jazz
640.q: That is true. But last year when Bob did his tributes to Sidney Bechet and he worked with Wynton Marsalis, all the musicians with Wynton were totally dedicated to what was going on. I think it’s because they didn’t have an interest in it. It’s not that they couldn’t do it. And I think maybe now…

340.t: Black audiences and students' interest in jazz
340.s: Mancuso blames lack of education and fluff-course attitudes for few black students and audiences, and recalls sharp New York recruits.
340.q: I think it’s a lot of lack of education, I really do. I don’t think they have — they haven’t taken many courses in anything like this, and — because I have black kids come and say man I never heard this kind of music. Because they’re into rap and hip hop, and it’s a faster pace and it’s — and…

347.t: Why black musicians have lost ground and the need for blunt lectures
347.s: He criticizes today's black musicians for assuming they have it, discusses opportunity and money for study, and offers to lecture candidly.
347.ch: Reflections on jazz, race and education
347.q: Michael Bolton. You wouldn’t get that in 1951 from — no chance. What happened? They discovered how to improvise. How to make it work. They paid attention. 64.t: Black institutions and universities neglect jazz
64.s: Taylor explains why few young African Americans enter jazz: schools ignore jazz and he gave up on working with them.
64.q: Well it’s deeper than that, unfortunately. One of the reasons you don’t have African- Americans in any number involved is that most of the traditionally black institutions ignore, in the same way that white institutions ignore jazz, for a variety of reasons. Most of the people who teach are trained…

610.t: Why jazz is undervalued and the college circuit
610.s: Vollmer sees jazz as black, syncopated and not classical, discusses conservatory training, and wishes for college bookings presenting jazz history.
610.ch: Jazz's place and the band's future
610.q: A good friend of mine from high school that I — he was the other jazz guy in the high school and we kept up for a long time, he felt like, you know Ben Webster should have been given a stipend of $10,000 a year in order to stay in the country so he didn’t have to live in Denmark.
